Didactic

/dih-DAK-tik/ — stress on DAK · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Didactic describes something meant to teach a lesson, often in a way that feels instructive or preachy.

The novel felt didactic, pausing every chapter to lecture the reader about honesty.

Worked Example

The children's book taught sharing through the story: the main character learned a lesson about kindness after being mean, and by the end it was clear the author wanted kids to absorb the moral. The book was didactic—designed to instruct as much as entertain.

didact (teaching/teacher) + -ic (having the character of) = having the character of teaching; meant to teach. The book's structure—lesson learned, moral stated—shows it's built to instruct, not just tell a fun story. Didactic captures that intentional teaching purpose.

How Didactic Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

instructive

instructive: intended to teach, in a neutral way

preachy

preachy: pushing a moral lesson in an annoying way

prescriptive

prescriptive: laying down rules about how things must be done

Antonyms

entertaining

entertaining: meant to amuse and delight, not to instruct

lighthearted

lighthearted: playful and fun, free of heavy lessons

How Strong Is It? — informative → educational → instructive → didactic

informative vs. didactic

informative vs. didactic: An informative poster simply presents the facts, while a didactic one lectures you about what to think of them.

educational vs. didactic

educational vs. didactic: An educational film teaches you something new, but a didactic film keeps stopping the story to hammer home its moral.

instructive vs. didactic

instructive vs. didactic: An instructive example shows you how something works; a didactic one insists on spelling out the lesson twice.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — didact

Root — didact: teach; teaching — from Greek didaskein, 'to teach' (didaktikos, 'apt at teaching') (Greek)

Suffix — -ic

Suffix — -ic: characteristic of; having the nature of (Greek (via Latin -icus))

Put it together

Put it together: didact- (teach) + -ic (characteristic of) = having the character of teaching. Something didactic sets out to teach you a lesson — often so determined to instruct that it forgets to entertain.

Use the root in a new word: autodidact

Use the root in a new word: autodidact: With no formal art classes, the painter was an autodidact who taught herself everything from library books.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal/academic

Reach for didactic when something is clearly designed to teach a lesson or instructive message—in a book, film, speech, or even a character's role. Be aware: the word often carries a negative edge, suggesting the teaching is heavy-handed or overwrites entertainment.
